http://www.bgnes.com/european-union/fico.text: BGNES European Union Fico warns EU against treating China as an enemy, rejects shortcuts for Ukraine Fico warns EU against treating China as an enemy, rejects shortcuts for Ukraine 26.08.2026 - 07:58 Share BGNES The Slovak prime minister said his country was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has urged the European Union to pursue "friendly" competition with China rather than treating Beijing as an enemy and erecting new trade barriers, CGTN reported. Fico made the remarks after talks in Bratislava with European Council President Antonio Costa, who began his annual tour of EU capitals in Slovakia. The Slovak prime minister said his country was concerned about the EU's ability to compete globally. He argued that improving competitiveness should not mean imposing new tariffs or barriers, but rather striving to achieve better results. "I have a different view of relations between the EU and China. I do not think we should fight China by erecting barriers and treating it as an enemy," Fico said. "China is a country with which we should compete in a friendly spirit and strive to be better." The two leaders also discussed the EU's next long-term budget, competitiveness, energy prices and the bloc's future enlargement. On the EU budget, Fico said Slovakia supports maintaining a strong cohesion policy to reduce regional disparities across the bloc. He also called for additional funding for eastern EU member states, particularly those sharing borders with Ukraine. "We even say that additional funding should be found for the countries in the eastern part of the EU that, for example, share borders with Ukraine," he said. Fico also identified a strong agricultural policy as another key priority for Slovakia. On EU enlargement, the Slovak prime minister reiterated his country's support for candidate countries seeking membership, but stressed that all applicants must meet the required criteria. "This means no exceptions and no shortcuts. And this also applies to Ukraine," Fico said. He argued that Ukraine should not be allowed to overtake countries such as Montenegro, Albania or Serbia in the accession process, noting that those countries have been preparing for EU membership for much longer. | BGNES Follow us also on Watch and Comment news Comment in X More from European Union EU allows Ukraine to use €90bn loan funds to buy Patriot interceptors 08.09.2026 - https://www.politico.eu/article/scottish.text: LIVERPOOL — Scottish Labour’s new leader, Michael Marra, said he does not believe there is a “realistic prospect” of the U.K. rejoining the European Union because of “huge political instability” across the continent. Speaking at the POLITICO pub during Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Marra argued that the changing political landscape in Germany and France meant the EU was not in a position to consider a British return “on any terms that we might think is reasonable.” Scotland’s governing Scottish National Party has repeatedly called for the U.K. to rejoin the bloc after 62% of Scots voted to remain in the EU in 2016. Advertisement Advertisement But Marra said that while he’d support a U.K. effort to rejoin should Europe find itself in a “different place” in the future, he admitted it may not be a “realistic prospect” for a generation or more. “Politics in Europe, I think, is really unstable at the moment. It’s facing many of the same challenges that we are in the U.K. in terms of the global economic instability, challenges in the Middle East, and migrant crises across parts of Europe have really destabilized politics.” Marra, who took over as leader after Labour suffered a humiliating defeat in May’s Scottish Parliament election, instead urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to be “pragmatic” about forging closer links with the bloc. “What we do need is a closer relationship because we know the economic cost that’s resulted from Brexit. I want to see us doing that on a case-by-case basis,” he said. “Some of the things we’ve done around Erasmus and so on, I think that is a key thing.” His comments come amid growing debate among senior Labour ministers about the next steps in the U.K.’s relationship with Brussels at the party’s annual gathering in Liverpool. In a major intervention ahead of the conference, former Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair said there should be a plan to rejoin a “reformed EU” in the next decade. Andy Burnham has not yet ruled out including conditions for a fresh membership bid in his party’s next election manifesto, but is expected to expand on his approach when he speaks to the Labour faithful later today. https://www.scottishlegal.com/articles/c.text: Article Tags: echr belarus Council of Europe renews call for Belarus to abolish death penalty 13 Oct 2026 Reading time: 2 minutes Article Tags: echr belarus The Council of Europe has called on Belarus to halt executions as part of renewed efforts to abolish capital punishment across Europe. The call came as the organisation held its first event at its Information Point for Belarusians in Vilnius, Lithuania, yesterday, marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, observed on 10 October. Belarus is the only country in Europe that still carries out executions. The Council of Europe has repeatedly opposed capital punishment in all circumstances. The Vilnius event brought together Council of Europe experts, diplomats and representatives of Belarusian civil society to discuss abolition. It forms part of the organisation’s work with Belarusian democratic forces and civil society, following the establishment of the Information Point in May 2026. A new website exploring the history of the death penalty in Minsk was launched at the event. It offers a virtual tour of locations associated with capital punishment in the Belarusian capital during the 20th and 21st centuries. Yuliya Ralko of the Belarusian National Youth Council (RADA) said: “The idea of this website came from the young participants of a workshop organised by the Council of Europe and RADA in May 2024 in Vilnius, as part of the Contact Group’s activities. We are very pleased to see this idea become a reality.” The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers adopted a decision on the death penalty on 7 October, condemning Belarus’s use of capital offences added to its criminal code in 2022 and 2023 to impose death sentences. It called on the Belarusian authorities to suspend all executions pending abolition and to apply alternative punishments already available under domestic law. The committee also welcomed a memorandum on abolishing the death penalty adopted by Belarusian democratic forces in June 2025. In a joint statement ahead of the World Day Against the Death Penalty, Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas reiterated their opposition to capital punishment in all cases and circumstances. https://www.dw.com/en/european-diplomats.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OtFN Prefer DW on Google Sergey Lavrov, under US sanctions for Russia's war on Ukraine, is photographed while he takes his seat at the G20 meeting Image: Erik S. Lesser/AFP Advertisement A Group of 20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta got off to a rocky start on Friday after top diplomats from European nations refused to take a "family photo" along with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is hosting the gathering, decided to scrap the photo before the meeting got underway because Washington didn't want it to become a spectacle or distraction. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters before the first session on Friday that there wouldn't "be a family photo with European partners and Mr. Lavrov together because ... there is no normalcy with Russia." The two-day gathering of the G20 grouping, which includes the EU, Russia, Germany, India, China, Brazil and other major countries, is meant to be a precursor to a G20 leaders summit later this December. That G20 leaders meeting in December is set to be hosted by US President Donald Trump at his golf club in Miami. G20 gathering is set to discuss issues like freedom of navigation in crucial trade routes and energy supplies Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pledged to "call on Russia to finally accept Ukraine's offer of a ceasefire, starting in the Black Sea" Image: Megan Varner/REUTERS Rubio stresses unity despite fractures Rubio still opened the talks by stressing unity on major issues, telling his counterparts that they were in a "critical moment." "We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he said. He pointed to disruptions to global energy and trade and said many were posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order." But several countries, including the United States and Russia, are involved in separate wars. Wars in Iran and Ukraine have resulted in a spike in food prices for people around the world . While the message is about unity and finding solutions to problems like freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Strait of Hormuz during the G20 meeting, the reality is that finding common ground will likely be much tougher. Given a renewed momentum to revive talks to end the war in Ukraine , there was also interest in getting Lavrov to talk about Russia's stance on future talks with Kyiv. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio appealed for unity between members of the G20, despite the US not inviting all of them to the ministers' meeting Image: Erik S. Lesser/AFP Russia willing to meet Zelenskyy in Moscow, Lavrov tells DW The US has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 meeting in Miami, but it's unclear whether Russia has accepted the invitation. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has previously said that he would be open to traveling to Miami to hold talks with Putin if he were also there. The Kremlin has so far declined direct meetings with Zelenskyy, with Russia's Sergey Lavrov telling DW on the sidelines of the meeting that Putin is willing to meet with the Ukrainian leader if he travels to Moscow. "President Putin said if he [Zelenskyy] is willing to meet, let him come to Moscow," Lavrov said. "We will guarantee his safety." Lavrov declined to say whether Putin will attend the G20 summit this December. Putin has not attended a G20 leaders meeting since 2019 and only attended a session virtually in 2023. Russia has also continued with its attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks , stepping up drone strikes on water and energy infrastructure. A Russian drone strike on a railway station in Dnipro on October 29 killed at least 14 people Image: Telegram channel on president ou Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyj EU top diplomat calls out Lavrov's 'lies' The European Union's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said ministers at the G20 meeting were able to call out Lavrov for his "lies" at the table. "We were talking about the big geopolitical crises, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head-on with this," Kallas said on the sidelines of the meeting. "Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives that we were also able to then rebuke," she said. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also called out Lavrov, saying, "If we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine." Lavrov says no easing of ties with US, 'no illusions' about diesel deal Lavrov, who is under international sanctions for Russia's war in Ukraine , was invited to the US at a time when the two countries have appeared to have fostered warmer ties. Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and also waived new sanctions on Russia's energy. The US announced the move just weeks away from the midterm elections on November 3. Lavrov said on Friday that despite those efforts, "in practice, no real progress in relations with the US has so far been seen." How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video South Africa, a founding member of G20, excluded from US meeting The Trump administration has been embroiled in disputes with South Africa , having imposed visa restrictions on South Africans who it said were complicit in discriminating against white people. Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year because US officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. But US officials didn't extend that invite to South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. "We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. With this many issues on the table, it appeared less likely that there would be a joint consensus at the end of the talks. Instead of a final declaration, the AFP news agency reported, the meeting is expected to end on Saturday with a chair summary drafted by the US. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/man-cro.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.10.26 15:31 Man crossed into Russia on Curonian Spit and was detained Translated by Karolis Broga Source: Elta EN Man crossed into Russia on Curonian Spit and was detained PHOTO: Jonas Balčiūnas | Elta Follow Delfi on Google A man walking through the dunes on the Curonian Spit on Sunday ignored warning signs and crossed into Russian territory, where he was detained, the State Border Guard Service (VSAT) said. Using the border surveillance system, officers from the Neringa border station spotted the man on the Baltic Sea coast on Sunday afternoon, the service said. He was walking through the dunes without carrying any large items before heading down to the shore and continuing towards Russia. The VSAT noted that bright yellow signs with text in several languages are in place both at sea and on land along the border with Russia, and the border protection zone is marked. The signs warn that the border protection zone lies ahead, with the border itself several hundred metres beyond them. According to the VSAT, the man is suspected of having ignored a sign marking the border protection zone as he walked towards Russia along the Curonian Spit. Patrols from the Neringa border station were dispatched to the scene, but by the time they arrived he had already walked several hundred metres along the shore towards Russia. He entered Russian territory shortly afterwards. "Some time later, we received information from Russia through border liaison channels that the man, reportedly a Polish citizen, had been detained by Russian border guards," the VSAT said in a press release. The VSAT has recorded the incident and is assessing the circumstances for a possible pre-trial investigation into an illegal border crossing. Border guards said incidents such as Sunday’s crossing along the seashore are very rare. They last recorded a similar crossing along the Baltic coast from Lithuania into Russia in 2018 and from Russia into Lithuania in 2017. https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: BRUSSELS — Hours before Andy Burnham arrived at a long-planned U.K.-EU summit Friday, it seemed like it’d be a humdrum victory lap. Talks ran late Thursday but that always happens; Britain seemed to believe everything was wrapping up as planned; Burnham even brought a super-delegation of seven Cabinet colleagues. “Deal done,” texted one U.K. official at 14 minutes to midnight. The spin war only came Friday morning — and not for the first time in Britain’s long Brexit saga, it arrived in a dry technical briefing in the European Council’s Europa building HQ. Advertisement Advertisement A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.” This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling. Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa. They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme. David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what. Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.” Advertisement Advertisement “The U.K. wanted to get something on Made in Europe, so that meant tuition fees being delayed as well. Somehow this has turned into a great defeat for the U.K. government because everything would be at the mercy of tuition fees,” he said. “That was what the U.K. government actually wanted.” Opposition politicians seized on the row, with Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage calling Burnham “naive.” Oliver Lewis, the former Conservative Brexit aide who has founded a new anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, said he had “been played like a fiddle by Brussels.” Brussels waffle If intended to seize the narrative, the statement worked. Other EU officials tried to downplay its significance as the morning unfolded — the key phrase “equal treatment” was, in fact, not in the final summit text — but the issue still dominated questions at a joint press conference by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. U.K. officials sprang up an unplanned briefing to counter-spin while Downing Street aides texted journalists with lines from a government spokesperson saying the deal was done. Burnham himself told the press conference: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done. It’s there in black and white.” A senior U.K. official insisted to POLITICO that the three deals on food standards, emissions and youth experience were not contingent on a pact on tuition fees. Advertisement Advertisement Yet EU diplomats continued to suggest they were part of a “package,” a concept neither Costa nor von der Leyen tried very hard to shoot down. (Von der Leyen told journalists merely that the tuition fees deal was “on a different sheet of paper,” before Burnham was treated to a battered fish lunch with a dessert of fruit with actual Brussels waffle.) Later Friday, Britain’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO he was “confident” that a tuition fees deal would be reached over the next six months. But the risk is not negligible. The six-month deadline to ink an agreement includes a French presidential election; if the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins it could have unpredictable results for the EU’s legislative agenda, including Made in Europe. And negotiations on the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (the legislation behind Made in Europe) are behind schedule, with talks between the Council and European Parliament yet to begin and disagreements over the automotive package adding to the complexity. Lower tuition fees, please The Commission and Council statement Friday morning seized the headlines for two reasons. The first was that it indicated the three deals tied up on Thursday night would not go ahead if Britain broke its promise to cut tuition fees. EU officials insisted they were not holding Britain “hostage,” but it was difficult to interpret the statement otherwise. The second was the phrase “equal treatment” — which appeared to suggest the whole deal was contingent on something Britain was not even willing to offer. Advertisement Advertisement Britain has signaled it will cut the international fees charged by U.K. universities — often well over £30,000 per year — to a lower level for students coming from the EU. But crucially, the U.K. has resisted European demands to match EU students’ fees with the £9,790-a-year “home fees” paid by U.K. students. Instead both sides have talked about a figure somewhere in the middle; negotiators have discussed a possible figure of £12,000 in private, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, who like others cited in this story were granted anonymity to share candid details. This is a deeply personal issue for many European politicians and diplomats, who either spent their youths at Britain’s famed elite universities — think Oxford, Cambridge or the London School of Economics — or now have children attending them, or hoping to, at least. There were immediate suspicions on the U.K. side that the EU’s statement was a piece of spin in the midst of a negotiation. The U.K. is holding its cards close on tuition fees to keep leverage over Made in Europe. A resolution on both issues was delayed because Made in Europe, designed to protect the bloc’s industries from a flood of cheap imports, remains in its early stages. The summit text agreed by the U.K. and EU contained no direct reference to the scheme, merely a pledge to “limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains.” Despite this, there was a view in the British contingent that the U.K. pushed the EU successfully for assurances on Made in Europe — meaning the EU had to flex its muscles somewhere else. Advertisement Advertisement “It was a pretty complicated discussion, and the British took a very hard line,” said one EU diplomat. This person added: “The discussion on tuition fees fell out because of the issue related to equal treatment… Ultimately, it’s not the statement we would have wanted, but with a partner like this, it’s important to maintain dialogue.” ‘Dear Andy’ Both sides put on smiles at the press conference, with Burnham calling the deals a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe.” Von der Leyen heaped praise on the man she referred to from the podium as “dear Andy.” Ultimately, the most important question about Friday’s row will be whether the deals Burnham announced are at any genuine risk of falling apart. “Six months seems a bit short to me” to sort out the tuition fees issue, said the EU diplomat quoted earlier in this story. British officials insist there is no issue. To make matters more complicated, Brussels is also pressing London to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, potentially tying this to Made in Europe provisions. The U.K. has yet to decide, though there is a widespread expectation among Labour MPs and some ministers that Britain will end up raising tariffs on Chinese EVs. If Friday’s deals do go ahead, the spin battle will be filed alongside countless other technocratic spats of the Brexit wars that fade into background noise. Advertisement But even so, the deals are not expected to see the light of day until at least 2028 — undercutting Burnham’s pitch to the British public that they will cut food costs and ease business red tape. (The prime minister highlighted Treasury analysis that showed Friday’s deals could add 0.5% or £17 billion to U.K. GDP.) Implementation of the agrifood deal is not planned until March 2028, while a deal to link the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems is only expected in the same year — meaning British firms will see no immediate relief from EU carbon border taxes, a further blow to the struggling steel industry. With the youth experience scheme not expected to be up and running until 2030, there are also questions over whether the program will survive the next election, which must happen before August 2029. There will be other challenges in selling the deal too. The U.K. claimed a late breakthrough on Thursday night in securing a role in shaping EU food standards rules — but hours later, Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds suggested Britain’s role would be limited. “We’d have experts in the room. We’d have the ability to put our point of view into that process. We’re not getting a vote because we’re not a member of the EU,” Reynolds told the BBC. Farage seized on this Friday, saying Britain would be forced to follow European rules on agricultural technology and pesticides rather than forging its own path. ‘Informal brainstorm’ Perhaps most importantly, Friday’s spin war is a reminder that nothing in Brussels is ever easy. It is a collision between Burnham’s big-picture way of doing politics and the EU’s hard, rules-based world. Advertisement This will matter for a prime minister who plans to stake much of his campaign at the next election on a battle for hearts and minds over Europe. That ballot isn't due until July 2029, but Farage predicted on Friday that the election would come as soon as May 2027, about a year after Burnham's ascent from the Greater Manchester mayoralty to Westminster. As POLITICO reported this week , the personally pro-rejoin Burnham has not decided exactly what to promise the British public — and is caught between his aspirational rhetoric and the reality of a divided Cabinet. Now he can throw in the difficulty of dealing with the EU too. Costa reflected this neatly in the press conference, telling Burnham he was “always welcome in the EU” — but almost in the next breath, reminding him that the EU’s principles, including the “indivisibility” of free movement from access to the single market, would “guide our engagement with the United Kingdom.” Burnham plans to set out the options he believes are available for the future relationship next month, tied in with his promised “10-year plan” for Britain. It will kick-start a conversation that will likely culminate in a Europe-shaped offer to the public in Labour’s election manifesto. But he also indicated Friday that he would not seek more policy-by-policy deals with the EU ahead of the next election, instead favoring a broader conversation. Even Starmer promised “iterative” deals once per year. The U.K. prime minister also continued to be vague about how that process would unfold. He spoke of “informal brainstorming” with the EU ahead of another summit next year. "We are open for brainstorming," Von der Leyen replied. Sebastian Starcevic, Sam Francis and Sam Blewett contributed reporting. Advertisement

https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/zele.text: Preşedintele american Donald Trump le-a spus liderilor europeni, în cadrul reuniunii Coaliţiei de Voinţă desfăşurate joi la Berlin, că Europa cheltuieşte prea mulţi bani pentru războiul din Ucraina şi că ar putea folosi aceste fonduri pentru propriile ţări după încheierea conflictului, a declarat sâmbătă preşedintele ucrainean Volodimir Zelenski, relatează Reuters . Trump a participat telefonic la reuniunea aliaţilor Ucrainei. Zelenski, care a luat parte la întâlnire, a spus că preşedintele american nu a formulat observaţia ca pe o ameninţare. „A spus că Europa cheltuieşte foarte mulţi bani şi că i-ar putea folosi pentru propriile ţări după încheierea războiului. Nu a sunat ca o ameninţare”, le-a spus Zelenski jurnaliştilor, înaintea unei întâlniri la Kiev cu ministrul britanic al apărării, Wes Streeting. Declaraţiile vin în contextul reluării discuţiilor privind încheierea războiului, după o pauză de nouă luni. Negocierile au fost reluate luna aceasta, la Abu Dhabi, iar Zelenski a salutat recentele declaraţii ale emisarilor americani privind implicarea Europei ca partener cu drepturi depline în procesul de pace. El a spus însă că partea americană trebuie să stabilească agenda şi data unei noi runde de discuţii. Preşedintele ucrainean s-a arătat totodată sceptic în privinţa disponibilităţii liderului rus Vladimir Putin de a face compromisuri. „Sunt puţin mai sceptic decât americanii în privinţa faptului că el este pregătit să facă compromisuri. Asta le-am spus, de altfel, şi reprezentanţilor echipei americane”, a declarat Zelenski. Putin nu a dat semne că ar renunţa la cererea ca Ucraina să cedeze întreaga regiune Donbas din estul ţării în schimbul păcii. Zelenski a respins această condiţie, amintind că numeroşi militari ucraineni au murit apărând teritoriul respectiv de la declanşarea invaziei ruse la scară largă, în 2022. Trump a declarat vineri, la întoarcerea la Washington, că Putin şi-ar fi exprimat clar dorinţa de a pune capăt războiului prin mijloace diplomatice. Zelenski a spus însă că nu este convins de intenţiile liderului rus şi a estimat că Moscova ar putea încerca să amâne o nouă întâlnire. Liderul ucrainean a reiterat că este pregătit să participe la reuniunea G20 pe care Trump urmează să o găzduiască luna viitoare, la Miami, şi că ar fi dispus să poarte acolo discuţii directe cu Putin. Până în prezent, Zelenski nu a primit o invitaţie. Zelenski s-a întâlnit la Kiev cu ministrul britanic al apărării, Wes Streeting, după un bombardament rusesc soldat cu moartea a două persoane, între care un băiat de şapte ani, în oraşul Krivoi Rog. Preşedintele ucrainean a descris vizita drept un semn important de solidaritate. Streeting a afirmat că declaraţiile lui Putin despre dorinţa de pace sunt contrazise de bombardamentele ruseşti. El a calificat, de asemenea, drept „o provocare revoltătoare” încălcarea spaţiului aerian polonez şi a îndemnat aliaţii să intensifice sprijinul pentru Ucraina. Ucraina doreşte „foarte mult” să adere la NATO, a declarat sâmbătă preşedintele Volodimir Zelenski, în condiţiile în care posibilitatea acordării unor garanţii de securitate pentru Kiev similare celor prevăzute de Alianţa Nord-Atlantică a revenit în centrul discuţiilor dintre statele occidentale, transmite France Presse, preluată de Agerpres. „Desigur, Ucraina doreşte foarte mult să fie în NATO”, le-a spus Zelenski jurnaliştilor, la Kiev, apreciind că aderarea la Alianţă reprezintă una dintre „cele mai evidente garanţii de securitate” pentru ţara sa. Tot sâmbătă, Zelenski a declarat că summitul trilateral din această săptămână, la care au participat liderii Chinei, Rusiei şi Statelor Unite, a fost „foarte nereuşit” pentru preşedintele rus Vladimir Putin. Potrivit liderului ucrainean, Putin nu a reuşit să recreeze Conferinţa de la Ialta, care a decis soarta Europei în 1945, relatează Reuters. Subiectul aderării Ucrainei la NATO, exclus de Washington începând din 2025, a revenit în discuţie în ultimele zile, în contextul unor noi negocieri pentru încheierea invaziei ruse, care durează de aproape cinci ani. Joi, la o reuniune desfăşurată la Berlin cu aliaţii Kievului, emisarul american Jared Kushner a declarat că Statele Unite ar putea fi dispuse să ofere Ucrainei „o garanţie de securitate similară celei prevăzute de articolul 5” al Tratatului Atlanticului de Nord. Această prevedere, care reprezintă unul dintre principiile fundamentale ale NATO, stipulează că un atac împotriva unui stat membru este considerat un atac împotriva tuturor aliaţilor. Prezent la aceeaşi reuniune de la Berlin, preşedintele francez Emmanuel Macron a pledat pentru reluarea discuţiilor privind aderarea Ucrainei la NATO. Vineri, Preşedinţia franceză a apreciat, la rândul său, că oferirea unei protecţii de tipul celei prevăzute de articolul 5 ar echivala, în practică, cu primirea Ucrainei în Alianţa Nord-Atlantică. Tot vineri, două rachete şi o dronă despre care există suspiciunea că ar fi ruseşti au căzut în sud-estul Poloniei, stat membru NATO şi vecin al Ucrainei. Secretarul general al Alianţei, Mark Rutte, a denunţat ulterior „încălcări grave” ale spaţiului aerian polonez. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News
